extracted.intended_audience: graduate students and researchers learning algebraic geometry (readers of Vakil's 'The Rising Sea')
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and tests for regularity and smoothness of schemes (including Jacobian tests, base-change checks, tangent-space computations), plus equivalences and properties of dimension-1 regular local rings / DVRs and Bertini-type generic smoothness results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Smoothness-Regularity Comparison Theorem
rubrics_metrics.description: If k is perfect, every regular finite type k-scheme is smooth over k. Every smooth k-scheme is regular (with no hypotheses on perfection).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Parts (a) and (b) are stated as Theorem 13.2.7. The text notes proofs are postponed but sketches the idea: An^k is regular, smooth varieties locally admit an étale morphism to An^k, and étale morphisms preserve regularity of local rings (Exercise 25.2.D). Keep in mind the field perfection hypothesis is used in the implication regular ⇒ smooth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Caution: regularity does not imply smoothness (over nonperfect fields)
rubrics_metrics.description: Regularity of a scheme does not necessarily imply smoothness over the base field if the field is not perfect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrative example: k = F_p(u), X = Spec k[x]/(x^p - u). The ring is a field (hence regular) but the Jacobian criterion fails (f'(u^{1/p}) = 0), so X is not smooth over k. Moral: smoothness is a relative notion depending on the base field; do not use 'regular' and 'smooth' interchangeably.

rubrics_metrics.name: Jacobian criterion for (non-)smooth points / regularity at k-valued points
rubrics_metrics.description: The Jacobian criterion characterizes non-smooth (singular) points of hypersurfaces/varieties by vanishing of the defining function and its partial derivatives; for projective hypersurfaces the non-smooth locus is given by f = ∂f/∂x0 = … = ∂f/∂xn = 0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For projective hypersurfaces if char k does not divide deg f (e.g., char 0) one can simplify checks using Euler's identity ((deg f) f = Σ xi ∂f/∂xi). The Jacobian criterion is emphasized as a primary practical tool for checking regularity at k-valued points (and is used to define tangent planes via linearization). Be cautious about characteristic-dependent exceptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regular local rings are integral domains
rubrics_metrics.description: If (A,m,k) is a regular local ring of dimension n then A is an integral domain (Theorem 13.2.11).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof given by induction on n: choose f ∈ m \ m^2, reduce dimension by passing to A/(f) and use Nakayama and prior exercises to show prime ideals must be zero. Consequence: geometric intuition that smooth points are locally irreducible is captured algebraically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regular point implies unique irreducible component through the point
rubrics_metrics.description: If p is a regular point of a locally Noetherian scheme X, then only one irreducible component of X passes through p (Exercise 13.2.K).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Related remark (13.2.L): a nonempty regular Noetherian scheme is irreducible iff it is connected. These are handy local-to-global observations when analyzing scheme structure near regular points.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regular embeddings: regular subschemes of regular schemes are regular embeddings
rubrics_metrics.description: If (A,m,k) is a regular local ring of dimension n and I⊂A cuts out a regular local ring of dimension d, then Spec A/I is a regular embedding in Spec A (Exercise 13.2.M(a)). If π:X→Y is a closed embedding of regular schemes, then π is a regular embedding (Exercise 13.2.M(b)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hint given: show I/(I∩m^2) has a k-basis given by r = n−d elements lifted to m, and show surjection by these generators yields dimension d regular local rings; use Exercise 12.1.D about surjections of integral domains of same dimension being isomorphisms. This provides a practical check for when a closed subscheme is a regular (local complete intersection-like) embedding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intersection codimension bound in smooth ambient (Exercise 13.2.N)
rubrics_metrics.description: If W is a smooth variety of pure dimension d over an algebraically closed field k, and X and Y are equidimensional subvarieties of codimensions m and n in W, then every component of X ∩ Y has codimension at most m + n in W.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof hint: use the diagonal ∆ ⊂ W ×k W as a regular embedding of codimension d and follow the rest of Exercise 12.3.E. The text warns that smoothness hypothesis on W cannot be completely dropped (Remark 13.2.12 gives a counterexample in a singular cone), so check ambient smoothness when applying such codimension bounds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Checking regularity at closed points by separable base change
rubrics_metrics.description: Suppose X is finite type over k and p ∈ X is a closed point with residue field k'. If k'/k is separable of degree d, then X_k (base change to k) is regular at the preimages p1,...,pd of p iff X is regular at p (Exercises 13.2.P and 13.2.14).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use tensoring of exact sequences on cotangent spaces: after base change dim_k TX_k,pi = d · dim_{k'} TX,p. In particular, regularity can often be detected after a separable field extension; for Galois extensions use transitive Gal(k'/k)-action to deduce regularity at one preimage suffices (Remark 13.2.15).

rubrics_metrics.name: Tangent plane / tangent line via linearization (Jacobian linear terms)
rubrics_metrics.description: If X ⊂ A^n is cut out by equations f1,…,fr and X is smooth of pure dimension d at a k-valued point a, then the tangent d-plane TaX is given by the r linear equations Σ_j (∂fi/∂x_j)(a) (x_j − a_j) = 0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This linear description is independent of choice of defining equations (Exercise 13.3.H). The Jacobian criterion ensures these r linear equations cut out a d-plane. This is the algebraic incarnation of the multivariable-calculus tangent plane and avoids epsilon-delta arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tangency criterion: multiplicity ≥ 2 implies containment in tangent plane
rubrics_metrics.description: If X ⊂ P^n_k is a degree d hypersurface cut out by f and L is a line not contained in X, and L meets X with multiplicity at least 2 at a k-valued regular point p ∈ X, then L is contained in the tangent plane to X at p (Exercise 13.3.L).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Geometric intuition: a line with higher intersection multiplicity at a smooth point is tangent; use local intersection/multiplicity computations to verify containment in the linear tangent space.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bertini's Theorem: general hyperplane section is smooth
rubrics_metrics.description: If X ⊂ P^n_k is a smooth subvariety of pure dimension d, then there exists a dense open subset U of the dual projective space P^n∨_k such that for every p = [H] ∈ U the hyperplane H does not contain any component of X and H ∩ X is smooth over κ(p) of pure dimension d−1 (Theorem 13.4.2).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof strategy: define the incidence variety Z = {(p∈X, H) : p∈H and either p is singular on H∩X or H contains X}, show the 'bad' hyperplanes form a closed set of dim ≤ n−1 (fibers are projective spaces of dim n−d−1), hence complement is dense open. Applications: existence of smooth hypersurfaces, and general hyperplane sections of a smooth variety remain smooth. Characteristic issues: some refinements/improvements are possible in characteristic 0 (Exercise 25.3.D/E).

rubrics_metrics.name: Dual variety properties
rubrics_metrics.description: The image of the incidence variety Z in P^n∨ is the dual variety of X. One expects dim(dual(X)) = n−1; classically the dual of the dual of X is X.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The incidence construction and rank conditions on the projective Jacobian matrix give the algebraic definition of the dual. Exercises illustrate the dual of a hyperplane is a point and the dual of a smooth plane conic is a smooth conic; duality reflects tangency relations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equivalences for Noetherian local rings of dimension 1 (characterizations of DVRs / regular local rings)
rubrics_metrics.description: For a Noetherian local ring (A,m) of dimension 1, the following are equivalent: (a) A is regular; (b) m is principal; (c) A is an integral domain and every ideal is of the form m^n (or 0); (d) A is a principal ideal domain; (e) A is a discrete valuation ring (DVR); (f) A is a unique factorization domain (UFD); (g) A is integrally closed in its fraction field.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text walks through the implications and proofs: regular ⇒ m principal (uniformizer), principal maximal ideal gives the chain of ideals m^n, discrete valuation arises from writing elements as unit·t^n, and integrally closed + Noetherian + dim 1 forces maximal ideal principal. These equivalences are central: in dimension 1 notions of regular, DVR, PID, UFD, integrally closed coincide under Noetherianness and integrality hypotheses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and basic properties of a discrete valuation and valuation ring
rubrics_metrics.description: A discrete valuation on a field K is a surjective homomorphism v: K^× → Z satisfying v(x+y) ≥ min(v(x),v(y)) (except when x+y=0). The valuation ring Ov = {x∈K : v(x) ≥ 0} is a local ring whose unique maximal ideal is {x : v(x) > 0}. When Ov is Noetherian it is a DVR.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Key examples: p-adic valuation on Q; valuation given by order of x in k(x); negative degree valuation in k(x) (1/x). Exercises show the valuation ring is local with unique maximal ideal, and that a DVR gives the usual uniformizer description: every nonzero element can be uniquely written u·t^n with u unit and n∈Z.

rubrics_metrics.name: Noetherian local rings: intersection of powers of maximal ideal is zero
rubrics_metrics.description: If (A,m) is Noetherian local then ⋂_i m^i = 0 (Proposition 13.5.2).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Geometric intuition: a function vanishing to all orders at a point vanishes in a neighborhood. The text notes Noetherianness is necessary (counterexample in analytic germs). This fact is used in arguments about chains of ideals and properties of dimension 1 rings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Zeros and poles at regular codimension-1 points via discrete valuations
rubrics_metrics.description: For a locally Noetherian integral scheme X, at any regular codimension-1 point p (where O_{X,p} is a DVR) there is a valuation v_p; for a nonzero rational function f, v_p(f)>0 means f has a zero of order v_p(f) at p, and v_p(f)<0 means a pole of order −v_p(f).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consequences/exercises: a nonzero rational function on an integral Noetherian scheme has only finitely many zeros and poles (Exercise 13.5.G). If a rational function has no poles it is regular (algebraic Hartogs Lemma, Exercise 13.5.H). Use these valuations to track divisors and orders of vanishing in dimension 1 and beyond.

rubrics_metrics.name: Normality does not imply regularity in codimension ≥ 2
rubrics_metrics.description: A Noetherian integrally closed (normal) scheme can still be singular in codimension 2; normality guarantees regularity in codimension 1 but not necessarily in higher codimension (Remark 13.5.12).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: the cone w z − x y = 0 is normal (Exercise 5.4.I(b)) but singular at the origin. Thus when checking regularity you must consider codimension: normality is weaker than being nonsingular everywhere.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tangent space naturality and coordinate-free viewpoint
rubrics_metrics.description: The definition of the tangent k-plane should be natural: for any automorphism σ of A^n_k, σ(T_pX) = T_{σ(p)}σ(X).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: You can verify this by hand on coordinates, but a cleaner approach is to interpret tangent space equations coordinate-free via the canonical identification of n-space with its tangent space at p and treating the Jacobian as a linear transformation cutting out T_pX independently of coordinates or defining equations (see Side Remark 13.3.4).
